stem: A 40-year-old woman presents 5 days after abdominal surgery. On examination, the surgical site shows a soft, fluctuant swelling without erythema, pus, or bleeding. The patient has no fever or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A soft fluctuant swelling without erythema, pus, fever or bleeding = seroma (serous fluid collection).

why.C: Would show erythema, pus or fever.

stem: 45 years old female taking anticoagulation because she had a valve replacement surgery a long time ago (forgot which surgery but it was laparotomy I think ) so they stopped her coagulation before surgery. 2 days after the surgery her anticoagulation was started again the nurse noticed the site of the wound was swollen and had skin color changes. When you examined it after pressing on the wound you noticed blood clots oozing from the wound site. What could be the cause?
srcNote: [Source formatting note: The last option was also labelled C; labels are displayed in sequence.] Choice A is written as "hamartoma" in the source; this wording and the original key are preserved.
expl: The source option "hamartoma" is a typo for HEMATOMA: swelling, skin discoloration and clots oozing from the wound after anticoagulation was restarted = wound hematoma.

why.B: Abscess would show pus, fever, erythema.
why.C: Seroma is clear fluid without discoloration; dehiscence shows separation/serosanguinous fluid.

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic man was hospitalized with right foot pain and 1 x 2 cm ulcer on his forefoot. Which of the following is the most important step in management?
srcNote: not sure (Skin,Soft tissue, Wound and Scars) Source keys differ or are marked uncertain. No replacement answer has been inferred. Other source key (Final 439 F Q42): A. Wound care. A Other source key (Final 437 A Q28): B. Wound care C. Revascularization B/C not sure Other source key (Final 434 F Q25 (p. 174)): A. Wound care. B. Revascularization. A/B not sure Other source key (Final 433 A Q25 (p. 182)): D. Revascularization. D (not sure) Davidson: if the blood supply is adequate, dead tissue can be excised in the expectation that healing will occur, provided infection is controlled and the foot is protected from pressure. If there is ischemia as well, the priority is to revascularize the foot, if possible.
expl: Source keys differ between versions (A, B/C, A/B, D). Wound care (debridement, offloading, infection control) is the base of every diabetic ulcer; but foot pain in a diabetic with an ulcer suggests ischaemia, and "if there is ischaemia, the priority is to revascularize" (Davidson, quoted in the source). Both A and D are accepted here.

why.B: Only if there is spreading infection/sepsis.
why.D: Accepted — most important when the limb is ischaemic.

stem: A patient who underwent surgery and during rounds the physician noticed serosanguinous discharge and upon pressure on the gauze the wound produced more serosanguinous discharge and the sutures were intact with a bulge. No pus or erythema was noticed. What is the cause?
expl: Serosanguinous ("salmon-coloured") discharge that increases with pressure, intact skin sutures and a bulge = fascial (partial) dehiscence — the classic warning sign.

why.D: Hematoma gives blood/clots, not serosanguinous fluid.

stem: A pt who had median sternotomy and developed a keloid scar, and asks about what to tell the pt to expect to have ?
srcNote: D ( wound management ) * The source key is written as "A-D"; it does not clarify whether this means A and D or all choices.
expl: Source key A (one version also marked D). Keloids are typically itchy and can be painful; they keep growing beyond the scar rather than fluctuating.

why.C: Can occur but itching is the classic symptom.
why.D: The alternative mark in the source.

stem: Patient has 1x2 diabetic ulcer on foot . Besides wound care what is the most important step in management ?
expl: Besides wound care, the most important step for a diabetic foot ulcer is restoring blood flow (revascularization) when perfusion is inadequate — no ulcer heals without blood supply.

stem: A 26 year old male sustained a 35% TBSA third degree burn. He is planned for multiple debridement and skin grafting procedures. The problem that there is no enough donor skin. What is the best technique to ensure that the donor skin available will be enough for the procedure?
srcNote: (Burn) Source note (Midterm 428 Q3): A. To reduce the donor ara. A Skin graft meshing: The mesh incisions allow the graft to be expanded to cover large defects when donor sites are limited.
expl: Meshing makes slits in a split-thickness graft so it can be expanded (e.g. 1.5:1 to 3:1) to cover a larger area when donor sites are limited. Allografts, xenografts and dermal substitutes are temporary covers.

why.D: Needs a graft on top later; doesn't increase donor skin.

stem: Patient had a superficial 3cm lipoma on forearm removed. Which of the following is the best method for subcuticular skin suturing?

opts.t: 3-0 vicryl, non cutting needle, subcuticular fashion

srcNote: ( practical procedure and investigations) Source note (Midterm 436 F Q10): A. 4-0 monofilament, cutting needle, subcuticular fashion A Other source key (Midterm 438 F Q24): Patient had superficial 7cm lipoma on the back removed, which of the following is the best method for skin suturing ? A. 0. Monofilament -non absorbable in subcuticular A (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients) Source note (Midterm 435 A Q3): (Cutting needles are used to suture skin. Davidson), (absorbable suture, such as Monocryl or Vicryl, is used [Source note ends here.]
expl: Skin is closed with a cutting needle; a fine (4-0) absorbable monofilament (Monocryl) in a subcuticular fashion gives the best cosmetic result and needs no removal.

why.A: Non-cutting (round) needles are for soft tissue/bowel; 3-0 Vicryl is braided and thicker.
why.C: Too thick; mattress sutures leave marks.

stem: You just complete an oncologic resection procedure on a patient and plan to start that patient on chemotherapy. How long should you ideally wait before starting the first cycle of chemotherapy to minimize the chances of wound healing problems?
srcNote: Related source keys and comments conflict on timing; the original statements are preserved. Other source key (Final 432 F • Repeated Qs list • Q26 (p. 224)): C. 6 weeks D. 8 weeks C or D not sure Other source key (Final 431 Q33 (p. 242)): ANSWER: B (Essentials of plastic: 14 days). Source note (Midterm 435 F Q6): (From a wound healing perspective the third phase of wound healing is completed by the third week and it is the phase most susceptible to factors that delay wound healing such as chemotherapy, thus starting chemotherapy after 3 weeks ensures wound healing does not get delayed, therefore the answer is B)(Essentials of plastic book had a question with the same scenario and the answer was to wait for 10-14 days to minimize healing problems)
expl: Chemotherapy impairs the proliferative phase of wound healing; starting ~3 weeks after surgery avoids wound problems (other sources say 10–14 days).

stem: Patient had small laceration of his forehead, 5-0 prolene cutting suture were used. the suture should be removed after how many days?
srcNote: (Face 3-5 days) (practical procedures and investigation of surgical patients) The source recalls give different removal intervals; the original choices and keys are retained below. Other source key (Midterm 436 A Q12): A. At least 2 Days A - Face 3-5 days Other source key (Midterm 435 F Q7): A. Day 5 A (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patient)
expl: Facial sutures are removed early (3–5 days) because the face is well vascularised and heals fast, and early removal avoids suture marks. The source recalls give 2, 4 and 5 days; the main key is 4 days.

stem: Which of the following is the longest phase of wound healing?
expl: Remodelling lasts from ~3 weeks to 1 year (or longer) — by far the longest phase.

stem: A 20 year old African American woman presented to the clinic complaining of swelling in the earlobe after 2 months of ear piercing. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: ( skin , soft tissue and wound management)
expl: A swelling of the earlobe months after piercing in a dark-skinned person = keloid.

stem: You are asked to see a 60 year old paraplegic patient with a sacral pressure sore measuring 10 x 10 cm. It has a healthy granulated bed. How would you manage this wound?
srcNote: Other source key (Final 432 F • Repeated Qs list • Q27 (p. 225)): C. Dressing changes until it heals C not sure
expl: A large (10 × 10 cm) sacral pressure sore with a healthy granulating bed won't heal reliably by dressings alone in a paraplegic → prepare the bed with dressings (and offloading), then close it surgically, usually with a local (rotation) flap. The source wrote "C not sure".

why.B: Too large to heal by secondary intention in reasonable time.
why.D: Local flaps are the standard; free flaps are rarely needed.

stem: An otherwise healthy patient with good nutritional status underwent gynecomastia excision Which of the following wound healing effects would be seen after prescribing multivitamins to the patient?
expl: Vitamin supplements improve healing only if the patient is deficient. In a well-nourished patient they have no effect.

stem: a Lady presented to you 4 weeks after ear piercing with a scar within the ear piercing. what’s the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Source key C. A raised scar confined to the piercing appearing within weeks = hypertrophic scar. Keloids usually appear later and extend beyond the wound.

why.A: Usually appears months later and grows beyond the wound.

stem: A Lady who will undergo elective plastic surgery , which of the following history information will affect the surgical results?
srcNote: Only two answer choices are provided in the source.
expl: Smoking (nicotine vasoconstriction, carbon monoxide) impairs skin/flap perfusion and wound healing — it directly worsens plastic-surgery results. An IUD has no effect.

stem: A patient presents to the plastic surgery out-patient clinic with a mild hypertrophic scar 4 weeks after primary wound closure in the forearm. What is the first line of scar treatment in this patient?

opts.t: Silicon sheeting and application of compression garments
Excision of the scar followed by radiation

expl: First-line for hypertrophic scars: silicone sheeting and pressure garments (non-invasive). Intralesional steroids come next; radiation is for recurrent keloids, not hypertrophic scars.

stem: a patient who had a single wound with one puncture in his forearm. Cleaning and debridement was done. What is the next step?
srcNote: (Skin, soft tissue, wound, and scars) Puncture wounds are never sutured duo to likelihood of infection (esp if duo to a bite)
expl: Puncture wounds (especially bites) are left open after cleaning and debridement because of the high infection risk; prophylactic oral antibiotics are given.

why.B: Never close a puncture wound primarily.
why.D: Not needed for a single clean-looking puncture.

stem: A patient presented with a 2cm*0.5 cm laceration on the forehead. How would you manage his injury after debridement of the wound?
expl: A clean, fresh facial laceration is closed by primary intention (well-vascularised face, best cosmetic result), without tension.

stem: A 65-year-old male presented with a scaly erythematous lesion with irregular borders on the dorsal left forearm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A scaly, erythematous, rough lesion with irregular borders on sun-exposed skin of an older man = actinic (solar) keratosis — a premalignant lesion that can progress to SCC.

why.B: Rapidly growing dome-shaped nodule with a keratin plug.
why.C: Benign adnexal tumour (turban tumour of the scalp).

stem: An otherwise healthy 32-year-old man who has a severe burn scar at the elbow. undergoes contracture release. Which of the following reconstructive methods is most likely to result in recurrent contracture?
expl: Split-thickness grafts have little dermis and contract most (secondary contraction), so contracture recurs. Flaps bring their own tissue and resist contraction.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis of the picture:
expl: Source key B. A crusted, ulcerated nodule on sun-damaged skin of an elderly face fits SCC (the source's comparison image shows SCC as a crusted nodule). BCC is classically pearly with telangiectasia and a rolled edge.

stem: A 40 year old diabetic patient who had a trauma and ended with deep laceration of his right arm which was sutured 8 hrs after the accident. The patient presented to the emergency 5 days afterwards with redness and pus discharge from the wound. We have opened and irrigated the wound and put it on a regular dressing. What is the expected change in the wound healing process?
expl: An infected wound opened and left to heal by secondary intention → the inflammatory phase is prolonged and the proliferative phase (granulation, contraction, epithelialization) takes longer.

why.C: Collagen is still made (more of it, slower).

stem: Which of the following is the most common type of melanoma?
expl: Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common type (~70%). Nodular is the most aggressive; acral lentiginous is commonest in dark-skinned people.

stem: Which ONE of the following is the main difference between Keloids and hypertrophic scars?

opts.t: Keloids extend beyond the original zone of injury

expl: Keloids extend beyond the original wound margins; hypertrophic scars stay within them.

stem: A 70 year old diabetic man who is bed ridden for the last 10 years, was brought to the emergency with history of sacral ulcer, which is 15 cm by 15 cm and 2 cm depth. On examination you can see pus discharge and necrotic muscles. How would you expect the wound healing phases to be affected?

opts.t: Decrease in the inflammatory and increase in the proliferative phase.
Increase in the inflammatory and decrease in the proliferative phase.
Increase in the inflammatory and proliferative phase.

expl: A large infected necrotic wound prolongs inflammation (bacteria, necrotic tissue) and, being a large defect healing by secondary intention, needs a long proliferative phase. Diabetes and immobility add to the delay.

stem: The top of the ladder of reconstructive plastic surgery is :
expl: The reconstructive ladder rises from simple to complex: secondary intention → primary closure → skin graft → local flap → distant flap → free flap (top).

stem: first ranked in reconstructive surgery ladder is:
expl: The first (simplest) rung of the reconstructive ladder is primary closure (some ladders put healing by secondary intention below it).

stem: hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of:
expl: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disease of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae, groin, perineum) — follicular occlusion with secondary apocrine involvement; the classic exam answer is apocrine sweat glands.

why.A: The modern view is follicular occlusion, but the keyed answer is apocrine glands.

stem: rodent ulcer “incomplete question”
srcNote: No answer key is stated in the source.
expl: "Rodent ulcer" is the classic name for basal cell carcinoma — a slowly eroding, locally destructive ulcer with rolled pearly edges (usually on the face). The recall gave only option A.
